The 10,260th meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is: the situation concerning Western Sahara. The agenda is adopted. In accordance with rule 37 of the Council's Provisional Rules of Procedure, I invite the representative of Algeria to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item 2 of the agenda. I wish to draw the attention of Council members to document S/2026/781, the report of the Secretary General on the situation concerning Western Sahara, and document S/2026/782, 2026/8/11, a letter dated 13 October 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council. Members of the Council have before them documents S/2026/868 and S/2026/870, each of which contains the text of a separate draft resolution. The Council is ready to proceed to the vote on the draft resolutions before it. I shall first put the vote the draft resolution contained in document S/2026/868, submitted by the United States of America. I shall put the draft resolution to the vote now. Will those in favor of the draft resolution contained in document S/2026/868, submitted by the United States of America, please raise their hand? Those against? Abstentions? The result of the voting is as follows: 11 votes in favour, 1 vote against, 3 abstentions. The draft resolution has not been adopted owing to the negative vote of a permanent member of the Council. I now give the floor to those members of the Council who wish to make statements after the vote. I give the floor to the representative of the United States.
Colleagues, to I think to talk about the future of this resolution and this mission, we should take a moment to remind everyone what the United Nations itself has been saying about the issue of a referendum for now for 30 years. And this is important to understand. As early as the mid 1990s, Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali didn't expect that the referendum would prove possible. In 1996, this council suspended voter identification, this council, because the parties could not agree on who should vote. In 1997, Secretary General Kofi Annan warned that the referendum may never happen at all. In 1999, Anan then reported that the prospect of holding a referendum was moving farther away, not closer. In 2002, Anan and his personal envoy, former Secretary of State James Baker, concluded that implementing the original settlement plan was, quote, “highly unlikely.” They even presented this council with the option of terminating MINURSO altogether as a result. In 2003, Anan warned that even if a referendum were held, The Security Council was highly unlikely to enforce its results. In '05, the director of MINURSO for five years, Eric Jensen, said that, quote, "The referendum called for the UN Security Council settlement plan of 1990-1991 has failed, will not happen." And in 2012, Bernard Miette, the former UN Undersecretary General for Peacekeeping, concluded that it was hard to see how it could be organized then or in the future. Colleagues, those are not our words. UN officials have been telling us this reality for 30 years, and here we are in 2026. And unfortunately, truly unfortunately, and not the intention of the United States, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter R for the referendum in the name that the United Nations hasn't even been preparing to hold for decades. Of course, the United States supports the principle of self-determination. There are many ways to realize and express the will of any given people. The United States has presented a resolution with the support of 11 members of this council, which would have taken historic steps, actually moving forward this 50-year frozen conflict to finally ending it, to realizing some results. We presented a path to finally stem the very real and devastating human cost of this conflict, a cost that was the very reason for the resolution that was vetoed today. In 2006, the Secretary General’s personal envoy warned that prolonging the deadlock could condemn another generation of Western Saharians to grow up in the refugee camps of Tindouf. Twenty years ago, colleagues. And now that generation has grown up. And we are taking the position that we should not have future generations and decades more of refugee camps. This is a resolvable conflict. And according to the UN's latest reports, just to understand the conditions, nearly two thirds, two thirds of children under five are suffering from anemia in these camps. One third have stunted growth. One in 10 receives only one in 10, 10% receives the minimum of an acceptable diet, 90% do not. So let's think about that again for a moment. That's 50 years of displacement, an entire lifetime and then some. Their children born as refugees, growing up as refugees, and now raising children as refugees. We will not support a status quo that condemns all of them, to another five decades. Last year's historic resolution 2797 finally established Morocco's autonomy proposal as the basis for negotiation, as a basis, and directed a strategic review of MINURSO's future mandate. We had three rounds of talks at a very high level. with all four parties, or two parties and observers at the table, excuse me, serious discussions about how to deliver genuine self-government, political representation, security, and a lasting settlement. We had further discussions about transition, about resource sharing, constitutional protections, international guarantees, demobilization, transition. And this resolution would have taken the next steps on that road to freedom and peace, but we had to do some things differently. Unfortunately, today, the unacceptable status quo, a status quo which the UN's own High Commissioner for Refugees has called, quote, "untenable, unsustainable, and genuinely, truly inhumane." The UN High Commissioner of Refugees calls the status quo inhumane. We will not lend our vote to business as usual in the face of such conditions, neither will we lend it to a mission whose very name perpetuates something that cannot be done. Even so, we are prepared to work, of course, with the Secretary General. Since this vote will result in a drawdown, we need to ensure that it be orderly and stable, that it protects UN personnel and addresses legitimate security and humanitarian needs. And we will continue to work with my co-chair, Personal Envoy de Mistura, and each of the concerned parties to find some way to negotiate a lasting peace. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the representative of the United States for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Bahrain.
Madam President, thank you. We express our regret that the draft resolution was not adopted despite the efforts made to reach a resolution that could contribute to a roadmap that could lead to a sustainable political solution. We thank the United States of America on its efforts in tabling the draft resolution. We stress, in this regard, the need for the content, the steps in this draft resolution that builds on resolution 2797, especially the adoption of the Moroccan initiative as a basis for the negotiations, and stressing that real self-determination under Moroccan sovereignty is the most applicable solution. We welcome the development of a framework for the UN mission that keeps pace with the political developments and promotes a final political solution that is sustainable. We welcome the renaming of MINURSO with dropping the “R” to reflect that we are keeping up with the current political developments and the Moroccan initiative in order to reach a final and sustainable solution for this issue. In conclusion, we value the efforts by the Secretary General and his personal envoy, Mr. Staffan de Mistura, in addition to all diplomatic efforts made by the United States of America to promote the political process. We stress the need to translate this progress to practical steps on the ground. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the representative of Bahrain for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of France.
Thank you, Madam President. Madam President, France strongly regrets the vote against by Russia for this resolution, which is geared towards renewal of the mandate of MINURSO. MINURSO plays a critical role for the stability in the region and to facilitate trust, which is necessary for advancement of the political process. Its abrupt closure would be exceedingly alarming in a context of resumed tensions. The draft resolution submitted by the United States was an important step forward for the advancement of the political process. The resolution 2797 adopted last year was a turning point for a lasting settlement to the conflict, and we regret the fact that the Council was unable to build upon that progress. We applaud the efforts undertaken by the Personal Envoy of the Secretary General and the United States to facilitate direct negotiations between the parties, and we reiterate our support. There is an overriding need for discussions to resume with a view to a negotiated solution, a just, sustainable, and mutually acceptable solution. Our position is well known. France – the question of Western Sahara is part of the Moroccan sovereignty, and as on the basis of the Moroccan plan, which we call for the reinitiation of discussions to arrive at a just, sustainable, and negotiated solution. Lastly, we deplore the rejection of this resolution by a member of the Council, expressing the support of the Council for the High Commissioner for Refugees for the establishment of sustained solutions for the Sahrawi refugees fully in accordance with refugee law. It is time. The status quo is not an option. Thank you.
France for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the United Kingdom.
Thank you, Madam President. The United Kingdom expresses immense disappointment at Russia's decision to veto this draft resolution. That decision undermines the Council's action on this file, jeopardizes the deployment of the UN mission, and risks setting back progress on the political process for the Western Sahara. We commend U.S. leadership on this resolution and welcome work of Personal Envoy de Mistura to advance the political process. We urge Council members to approach the question of Western Sahara in the interests of accelerating progress towards a just, lasting, and mutually agreed solution that meaningfully provides for self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. We reiterate our position that Morocco’s 2007 autonomy proposal is the most credible, viable, and pragmatic basis for a lasting resolution of the dispute. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United Kingdom for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Panama.
Thank you, Madam President. We regret the fact that this Council was not able to agree on the resolution on MINUSO. Panama voted in favor. We are convinced that the document provided an opportunity to preserve the necessary conditions on the ground and to support the renewed diplomatic momentum on issues pertaining to Western Sahara. I would like to thank the United States as the penholder for stepping up and in their consistent belief in dialogue and the efforts that they made to make amendments to the document. Panama voted in favor of the resolution. We are convinced that the current moment offered a significant opportunity to transform the renewed diplomatic momentum into substantive political progress. After years of deadlock, the meetings that were held at the beginning of this year in Washington and Madrid provided the parties with an opportunity to exchange positions and to explore possible means to move forward, to bring or to find common ground. It was critical to preserve this momentum and to provide it with continuity through sustained political commitment and active support from the United Nations. Panama believes that the Moroccan autonomy proposal presented in 2007 is the most viable foundation for negotiations to be resumed. At the same time, A lasting solution should emerge from a genuine political process between the parties, in line with the UN Charter and international law, including the principle of self-determination. Our own history reminds us of the importance of peoples being able to decide their future. That is why we think it is critical that the process makes headway through dialogue and compromise, without trying to pre-empt the outcome of any negotiations. We believe that that possibility still exists. We welcomed the inclusion in the text of the participation of a broad diversity of Sahrawi stakeholders, including those who are located in the territory, in the Tindouf camps and the diaspora. We believe this consultation process be critical to achieve a broader understanding of the aspirations and perspectives of the Sahrawi people and how they can determine their future. This, bearing in mind that holding a referendum seemed to be an illusory prospect, almost mission impossible. That is why we believed that it was important to bear in mind other opportunities and other options that would fulfill the principle of self-determination, to leave the door open for consultations for that possibility to be achieved. The human dimension cannot remain outside political efforts. We welcomed references in the text to the UNHCR and its High Commissioner, Mr. Salih, and we stressed the importance of meeting the needs of refugees, ensuring dignified living conditions and moving forward prospects for their future. Panama wanted to advocate renewing the mandate, extending the mandate for an additional year. While work is done on a political agreement and the current conditions persist on the ground, the presence of the United Nations will remain necessary to contribute to stability and to following up the ceasefire. Madam President, the challenge that we have before us was to turn this opportunity, this diplomatic opportunity, into a sustained process to achieve concrete results. We do hope that that possibility will continue. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Panama for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Latvia.
Thank you, Madam President. Latvia voted in favour of this resolution to extend the mandate of MINURSO, which has been a key stabilizing presence in Western Sahara for more than three decades. We regret Russia's decision to cast a veto and that the resolution was consequently rejected at a critical moment for the political process. We appreciate the efforts of the United States as penholder to advance a resolution on this long-standing conflict. We thank them for their engagement throughout the negotiations, addressing and accommodating some of the concerns of the Council members. leading to a more balanced text that better reflects the complexity of the conflict. Adopting this resolution would have ensured continuation of the momentum generated by resolution 2797. Members of the Security Council hold differing views on the autonomy proposal and the parameters of the future political solution, and we wish to make it clear that our vote in favor of this resolution did not constitute recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara or endorsement of the autonomy proposal as the predetermined outcome of the political process. And we reiterate our longstanding position that any solution must be just, lasting, mutually acceptable, and in accordance with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including the right of self-determination, consistent with the approach repeatedly affirmed by the Security Council. As a country whose own history is closely linked to the exercise of self-determination, we believe that the voices and aspirations of the people of Western Sahara should remain central to the political process. Madam President, through this resolution, the UN Security Council would have outlined a way forward. renew momentum in this political process. The current outcome undermines the process and puts at risk the continuity of the mission at a time when its presence on the ground remains essential. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Latvia for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Colombia.
Thank you, madam President. Colombia regrets the fact that the resolution was not adopted. And it also recognizes the efforts of the United States in building consensus throughout the process. We consider the resolution contributes to the common objective of advancing towards a solution to the question of Western Sahara. In particular, we believe that the principles that were highlighted in the resolution, self-determination, but also sovereignty, are commensurate with the values and the principles of Articles 1 and 2 of the UN Charter. In that context, our country considers that Morocco's autonomy proposal was the basis really for achieving a lasting political solution. Colombia encourages the parties to continue in good faith discussions with a view to reaching a solution that contributes to the stability and development of the region. We also call the attention of the situation in the Tinfouh camps requires, of course, renewed attention from the international community. My delegation welcomes the provisions that were in the resolution relating to the work of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the representative of Colombia for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Liberia.
Thank you, Madam President. Liberia voted in favor of this resolution because we believe it offered the clearest and most credible pathway toward a peaceful resolution of the long-standing dispute over Western Sahara. Our vote reflected a firm conviction: The Council must help turn decades of diplomatic effort into an achievable political settlement. The passage of time cannot substitute for progress toward peace. And we had hoped our position would have been very clear. We support Morocco's autonomy proposal. We welcome the resolution's recognition that genuine autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty presents the most feasible solution to the question of Western Sahara and its identification of the proposal as the only basis for negotiation. Clarity is not the abandonment of diplomacy. It is what gives diplomacy direction. Our hope, therefore, was that that direction will be matched by serious engagement and full cooperation with the facilitators, allowing for responses on the basis of the autonomy proposal. Again, Madam President, our belief was that the resolution would have moved the parties to seize the opportunity to negotiate in good faith. Liberia was motivated to vote affirmatively because operative paragraph 8 reaffirmed the Council’s commitment to a just, lasting, and mutually acceptable political solution in accordance with the principles and purposes of the United Nations Charter, including the principle of self-determination. Madam President, we were hopeful that today’s vote would establish a direction. Its value would then be measured by the progress that follows. Notwithstanding, for the people of Western Sahara and the region, we cannot and must not lose hope. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Liberia for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Pakistan.
Thank you, Madam President. Pakistan recognizes the efforts undertaken by the United States as the penholder to bridge gaps and accommodate various perspectives highlighted by the Council members during the negotiations. We also acknowledge the efforts of the United States in striving to achieve a political resolution to this long-standing dispute. Our abstention on this resolution is consistent with our long-held position on this important issue. We continue to believe That lasting peace in the region can only be achieved through a mutually acceptable political solution, through dialogue and consensus among the parties. Such a solution must be consistent with the principles and purposes of the UN Charter, providing for self-determination, as reflected in relevant UN resolutions. The cardinal principle of self-determination, enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and grounded in international law, must remain sacrosanct and inviolable. We also support the continuing stabilizing role of MINURSO. Any evolution in the mission’s mandate or configuration should support and be guided by progress in the political process and conditions on the ground. Pakistan has been and will continue to support all political efforts for just and lasting peace in the region. and expresses the hope that all concerned parties will engage in negotiations in good faith. We also hope that any ongoing efforts will help to genuinely reflect the aspirations of the people of Western Sahara for their future and command the confidence of all stakeholders. Durable peace, stability, and prosperity of the entire region should remain our shared objective. I thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Pakistan for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Somalia.
Thank you, Madam President. Somalia abstained in the vote of the draft resolution S/2026/868 concerning the renewal of MINUSO’s mandate. We welcome the renewed efforts of the Secretary-General’s personal envoy and the resumption of the direct dialogue. We also acknowledge The United States has a penholder's role in facilitating recent diplomatic engagement. Last year, Somalia voted in favor of the resolution 2797 of 2025. It's from our belief that the established framework under the resolution deserves sufficient time and sustained engagement. Additionally, the momentum it created, however modest, should be preserved and built upon. Our abstention on this resolution today reflected concern that some of the provisions could prejudge the outcome of the negotiations. A just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution cannot be predetermined. It must emerge through a genuine dialogue and compromise, with due regard to the interests and aspirations of the people of Western Sahara, and in accordance with the purposes and the principles of the United Nations Charter and relevant Security Council resolutions. Somalia attaches great importance to MINUSC’s role in helping to de-escalate tension, preserve stability, and maintain conditions conducive to political process. We encourage Council members to continue consultation in a constructive spirit with the aim of reaching agreement on the Mission’s mandate. In the meantime, all concerned should exercise restraint and avoid steps that could undermine stability or the prospects of the dialogue. In closing, Somalia remains committed to supporting the Secretary-General and his personal envoy, Mr. Staffan Mistura, in facilitating political process under United Nations auspices. We urge all concerned to engage in good faith. The Council must remain united in its support for a peaceful negotiated settlement of the question of Western Sahara. I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the representative of Somalia for the statement. I shall now give the floor to the representative of China.
Thank you, President. China abstained on the draft resolution just put to vote, I would like to explain China's positions as follows. Over the years, MINUSO has earnestly carried out the council mandate, playing an important role in maintaining stability on the ground, preventing escalation, and protecting civilians, thereby creating favorable conditions for advancing a political solution to
